messages:
oliver: Heads-up — seeing a recurring ~200ms write latency jitter on local NVMe on a subset of gnodes across ap-southeast1 and us-west1 over the last 12h. Correlates with increased GPU attach failures during batch launches. Logs below.

oliver: ```
node=gnode-az3 id=gn-12345 nvme_write_ms=187,13,9,201,11,8,190,12
metric: gpu_attach_fail_pct +3.4% (window aligned with spikes)
``` 

jess: ugh. are these firmware-level retries or host-side queueing? any SMART flags? :thinking_face:

oliver: SMART looks mostly green, temp stable. pattern looks like a "write-train" — bursts of small writes from janitor + scheduler metadata sync aligning with background scrub window. Not random flashes.

tara: do we have region rollout/maintenance that could have nudged CPU/irq balancing? ap-southeast had a peering flit at ~1745551200 but not sure if related.

kevin: can we repro with a synthetic smallwrite workload? if janitor is the culprit, pushing a controlled scrub will show it.

oliver: ran a 15m micro-bench: `fio --name=smallwrite --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --iodepth=16 --numjobs=4` — perf oscillates with same cadence.

sre-bot: Alert: nvme_write_latency_spike on 7 nodes in ap-southeast1 (detected 1745556500). Creating incident stub.

jess: interestingly spikes line up with janitor cron at :15 and :45. can we temporarily deschedule janitor on those pools for next hour and observe?

tara: +1. descheduling will risk backlog but lets see impact. @kevin can you flip janitor concurrency to 0.2x for pool-ephemeral-asia and pool-ephemeral-west in prod2? keep a rollback plan.

kevin: doing it now. command: `opsctl rollout janitor --pool pool-ephemeral-asia --concurrency 20% --dry=false` — rolling over 24 nodes.

deploy-bot: Rollout started for janitor concurrency change (id=rb-20240310-21). Stagger 10s per host.

oliver: after ~3 minutes latency spikes amplitude dropped to 30-40ms, gpu attach failures back to baseline. provisional correlation stronger.

jess: good. long-term we probably want write coalescing in janitor or a low-priority ioclass so smallwrites don't thrash the scheduler. also consider bumping write-back throttles for overlayfs.

tara: cost tradeoff: reducing janitor concurrency increases cleanup time ~3x on affected pools which pushes some ephemeral reclaim to on-demand GC (possible extra egress and storage ops). estimate incremental cost ~ $2.4k/week if sustained — we should quantify.

kevin: logged quick experiment: restoring full concurrency doubles the spike amplitude within 90s. keeping 20% seems safe for next 6 hours while we run mocks.

jess: can we add a short-term mitigation: pin affected GPU attach routes to nodes in different racks where janitor cadence is staggered? routing logic can avoid hotset.

oliver: yes, smart-routing policy can prefer gnodes with last-janitor-run > 10m. i'll open a PR for a soft preference.

sre-bot: Note: incident stub updated with mitigation steps and experiment links. tagging oncall.

kevin: also found a cheap firmware knob on a vendor build that disables aggressive NVMe power-state transitions during sustained smallwrite bursts — vendor says it reduces the spikes, but requires a host reboot and vendor approval. vendor ticket: VT-9821.

tara: rebooting fleet is heavy; prefer scheduling per-node toggles during maintenance windows. vendor risk: unknown impact on lifetime but could help.

jess: short plan:
1) keep janitor concurrency at 20% for affected pools for 6-12h
2) apply routing preference to avoid recently-scrubbed hosts
3) run extended fio workload to validate
4) evaluate vendor firmware toggle on a small canary and measure

kevin: executing step 1 now (completed), step 2 pr opened: https://git.redwood/repo/PR-3812

oliver: after 1h of low-concurrency we saw roughly 70% reduction in high-amplitude spikes and attach failure delta gone. tagging this as "mitigated" for now. :white_check_mark:

jess: thanks. next actions: cost calc (tara), janitor code changes to coalesce small writes (oliver + eng-runtime), vendor canary schedule (kevin). we'll reconvene if spikes return. :thumbsup:
